question.text: Is driving in New Jersey a right or a privilege, and what can state law do for certain violations?

answer.text: Driving is a privilege rather than a right, and state law allows or requires suspension for certain violations, on top of possible fines and imprisonment.

teaching.text: Because driving is a privilege and not a right, a suspension can be added on top of any fine or jail time, not used in place of them. Remember: privilege, not a right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving is a privilege rather than a right, and state law allows or requires suspension for certain violations, on top of possible fines and imprisonment.

question.text: What are the grounds for losing the driving privilege in New Jersey?

answer.text: Grounds for losing the privilege include unanswered or unpaid parking tickets, driving while suspended, no proof of insurance, physical or mental disqualification, drug or alcohol use, traffic violations, fault in a fatal crash and ignoring an MVC notice.

teaching.text: The list mixes paperwork and behavior, so an unpaid parking ticket or an ignored MVC notice can threaten the privilege just as a traffic violation can. Remember: tickets, insurance, health, alcohol, crashes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Grounds for losing the privilege include unanswered or unpaid parking tickets, driving while suspended, no proof of insurance, physical or mental disqualification, drug or alcohol use, traffic violations, fault in a fatal crash and ignoring an MVC notice.

question.text: Are all suspensions mandatory, and who decides the ones that are not?

answer.text: Some suspensions are not mandatory and are decided case by case by the MVC Chief Administrator or the courts.

teaching.text: Not every suspension is automatic; the MVC Chief Administrator or the courts weigh some of them case by case. Remember: some suspensions are judgment calls.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Some suspensions are not mandatory and are decided case by case by the MVC Chief Administrator or the courts.

question.text: What may the MVC Chief Administrator order to help decide whether to suspend a problem driver?

question.text: What makes a driver a habitual offender?

answer.text: A habitual offender is a driver whose license has been suspended three times within three years.

question.text: What can happen to a person who owes six months or more of child support or court-ordered health coverage?

answer.text: Owing six months or more of child support or court-ordered health coverage can lead to a court-ordered suspension of both driver and professional licenses.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Owing six months or more of child support or court-ordered health coverage can lead to a court-ordered suspension of both driver and professional licenses.

question.text: How old must a person be to buy, possess or drink alcohol in New Jersey, and who else faces consequences?

question.text: What penalties apply to a first DUI with a BAC of zero point zero eight percent but under zero point one zero percent?

question.text: How does the fine change for a first DUI with a BAC of zero point one zero percent or higher?

answer.text: For a first DUI with a BAC of zero point one zero percent or higher, the fine rises to three hundred dollars to five hundred dollars.

question.text: How do the fines compare for the two first-DUI BAC tiers?

answer.text: A first DUI between zero point zero eight and under zero point one zero percent is fined two hundred fifty dollars to four hundred dollars, while a first DUI at zero point one zero percent or more is fined three hundred dollars to five hundred dollars.

question.text: What annual surcharge comes with a first DUI offense?

answer.text: A first DUI offense also carries an annual surcharge of one thousand dollars for three years.

question.text: What does the IDRC charge for a twelve-hour program and for a forty-eight-hour program?

answer.text: The IDRC charges two hundred sixty-four dollars when the program lasts twelve hours and three hundred twenty-one dollars when it lasts forty-eight hours.

question.text: Who must be detained at an IDRC, and what happens there?

answer.text: Anyone charged with an alcohol-related traffic offense must be detained at an IDRC, where offenders take an alcohol and highway safety education program and are evaluated for treatment needs.

question.text: Which IDRCs serve first-time, second-time and third-time offenders?

answer.text: Each of New Jersey's twenty-one counties has an IDRC for first- and third-time offenders, while second-time offenders go to one of three regional IDRCs.

question.text: How do county IDRCs differ from regional IDRCs in who they hold?

answer.text: First- and third-time alcohol offenders are detained at their county IDRC, whereas second-time offenders go to one of the three regional centers.

teaching.text: The split is not first versus repeat; it is first and third at the county, second at one of three regional centers. Remember: second-timers travel regional.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: First- and third-time alcohol offenders are detained at their county IDRC, whereas second-time offenders go to one of the three regional centers.

question.text: What happens to an IDRC offender who is found to need treatment?

answer.text: Offenders found to need treatment are referred for a program of at least sixteen weeks, and satisfactory participation is a condition for getting licensed again.

teaching.text: Treatment is tied to the license, because satisfactory participation is a condition for getting licensed again. Remember: treat first, license later.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Offenders found to need treatment are referred for a program of at least sixteen weeks, and satisfactory participation is a condition for getting licensed again.

question.text: What does New Jersey's implied consent law mean for anyone driving on its roads?

answer.text: Under New Jersey's implied consent law, simply driving on New Jersey roads means agreeing to a breath test by police or hospital staff after an arrest for intoxicated driving.

teaching.text: The agreement comes from the act of driving on New Jersey roads, not from a signature or a promise at the roadside. Remember: driving here means consenting.

question.text: What happens to a driver who refuses the breath test?

answer.text: A driver who refuses the breath test is detained and taken to a hospital, where staff may draw blood.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A driver who refuses the breath test is detained and taken to a hospital, where staff may draw blood.

question.text: What surcharge comes with refusing a breath test?

answer.text: Refusing a breath test carries a violation surcharge of one thousand dollars a year for three years.

question.text: What does a refusal conviction tied to a first offense do to driving privileges?

answer.text: A refusal conviction tied to a first offense means losing driving privileges until an ignition interlock device is installed.

question.text: How does an ignition interlock device stop an impaired driver?

answer.text: An ignition interlock device has a built-in breathalyzer that stops the vehicle from starting when the driver's BAC is above zero point zero five percent.

teaching.text: The device checks the driver's breath before the car will start, and it blocks the start above zero point zero five percent. Remember: blow before you go.

question.text: How does the adult DUI limit compare with the BAC level that an installed interlock blocks?

answer.text: The adult DUI limit is a BAC of zero point zero eight percent, but an installed interlock blocks the engine once BAC tops just zero point zero five percent.

teaching.text: The interlock line is lower than the adult DUI limit, so a driver can be under zero point zero eight and still be blocked. Remember: the device is stricter.

question.text: How long must the interlock stay installed after a first DUI from zero point zero eight to under zero point one zero percent?

answer.text: After a first DUI with a BAC of zero point zero eight to under zero point one zero percent, the interlock stays installed for three months from restoration of driving privileges.

question.text: How long is the interlock required after a first DUI from zero point one zero to under zero point one five percent?

teaching.text: The middle tier falls between the others: longer than three months, shorter than the high-BAC term of twelve to fifteen months. Remember: middle tier, up to a year.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After a first DUI with a BAC of zero point one zero to under zero point one five percent, the interlock is required for seven months to one year after restoration.

question.text: When is the interlock required after a first DUI at zero point one five percent or higher?

answer.text: After a first DUI at zero point one five percent or higher, the interlock is required during the suspension and for twelve to fifteen months after restoration.

teaching.text: At the highest first-DUI tier the interlock is needed during the suspension too, not only after privileges are restored. Remember: during and well after.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After a first DUI at zero point one five percent or higher, the interlock is required during the suspension and for twelve to fifteen months after restoration.

question.text: How does the interlock term for a breath-test refusal compare with the term after a first DUI at zero point one five percent or higher?

answer.text: For a breath-test refusal, the interlock runs for nine to fifteen months after restoration, compared with twelve to fifteen months after a first DUI at zero point one five percent or higher.

question.text: How long is the interlock required after a second or later DUI or refusal offense?

answer.text: After a second or later DUI or refusal offense, the interlock is required during the suspension and for two to four years after restoration.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After a second or later DUI or refusal offense, the interlock is required during the suspension and for two to four years after restoration.

question.text: For offenses on or after February nineteen, two thousand twenty-four, what may a person arrested for certain alcohol offenses choose to do?

question.text: What happens to someone who drives after failing to install a court-ordered interlock?

question.text: What are the penalties for a first, second and third offense of driving while suspended?

question.text: What penalties apply to driving while suspended for a DUI, a refusal or as a habitual offender?

question.text: What kind of offense is driving while suspended for a second or later DUI or refusal conviction?

question.text: What does an owner face for knowingly letting someone drive whose license is suspended for DUI or refusal?

question.text: What fines does an unsafe driving conviction carry for a first, second and third or later offense?

question.text: What can a first reckless driving offense bring?

question.text: When are fines doubled in a sixty-five miles per hour zone?

question.text: In which two kinds of places do fines double for moving violations?

question.text: What is the penalty for failing to pass a vulnerable road user with due caution, with and without an injury?

question.text: What does a driver face for ignoring a police officer's request to light up the driver's compartment during a stop?

question.text: What are the fines for carrying an open alcohol container or an unsealed cannabis item in the passenger area?

question.text: What fine applies for failing to clear snow or ice from a vehicle before driving, even if none of it comes loose?

question.text: What fines apply when ice flies off a vehicle and causes death, injury or property damage?

question.text: What penalties apply for leaving a vehicle on or along a limited-access highway for four hours or more without permission?

question.text: How do the penalties change for repeat vehicle abandonment?

question.text: What can insurance application or claim fraud bring, and what does an auto insurance crime conviction cost?

question.text: What are the penalties for lying on a license or registration application?

question.text: What are the penalties for having someone else take your license test, or taking it for someone else?

answer.text: Having someone else take your license test, or taking it for someone else, brings a two hundred dollars to five hundred dollars fine, thirty to ninety days in jail, or both.

teaching.text: This rule punishes both sides, the person who sends a stand-in and the stand-in, and its jail range differs from lying on an application. Remember: your test, your seat.

question.text: What happens to a boater convicted of DUI on New Jersey waters?

answer.text: A boater convicted of DUI on New Jersey waters loses boating and all driving privileges, and a first offense is fined two hundred fifty dollars to five hundred dollars.

teaching.text: A DUI on the water reaches the road as well, because the boater loses all driving privileges along with boating privileges. Remember: drunk boating sinks driving.

hooks_spoken: Driving is a privilege, so New Jersey can suspend it for violations as well as fine or jail the driver.

Unpaid tickets, missing insurance proof, alcohol or drug use, fault in a deadly crash or an ignored MVC notice can all cost the privilege, and some suspensions are weighed case by case, sometimes after a re-examination.
Three suspensions inside three years make you a habitual offender, and six months of unpaid child support can cost both your driver and professional licenses.

hooks_spoken: Alcohol is off limits under twenty-one, and an underage buyer or drinker at a licensed place risks a five hundred dollar fine and a license loss.
Even a BAC of zero point zero one can bring an underage suspension of thirty to ninety days, starting at eligibility or conviction, whichever comes later.
Expect fifteen to thirty days of community service plus an IDRC or an alcohol education and highway safety program as well.

hooks_spoken: A first DUI under zero point one zero is fined two hundred fifty to four hundred dollars, and at zero point one zero or higher the range moves up to three hundred to five hundred.
On top of that comes one thousand dollars a year for three years, plus the IDRC bill of two hundred sixty-four or three hundred twenty-one dollars.

First and third offenders are detained at their county IDRC, second offenders at a regional one, and anyone who needs treatment must take part satisfactorily in a program of at least sixteen weeks before getting licensed again.

hooks_spoken: Driving on New Jersey roads already counts as agreeing to a breath test after an arrest for intoxicated driving.
Refuse it and you are taken to a hospital where blood may be drawn, you owe one thousand dollars a year for three years, and a first-offense refusal keeps you off the road until an interlock goes in.

hooks_spoken: The interlock will not start the car above zero point zero five, a stricter line than the adult limit of zero point zero eight.
After a first DUI the interlock term grows with BAC: three months, then seven months to a year, then the suspension plus twelve to fifteen months.
A refusal means nine to fifteen months, a repeat offense two to four years, installing early may cut penalties, and driving without a court-ordered device adds a year of suspension.

hooks_spoken: Driving while suspended starts at five hundred dollars and more suspension, then climbs to seven hundred fifty with jail and one thousand with ten days in jail.

When the suspension came from a DUI, a refusal or habitual offending, the extra suspension is one to two years, a first school-zone offense brings sixty to ninety days in jail, and driving while suspended for a second or later DUI or refusal is a fourth-degree crime.
An owner who knowingly hands the keys to such a driver can lose license and registration and pay a fine, serve jail time or both.

hooks_spoken: Unsafe driving fines rise with each offense and always carry a two hundred fifty dollar court surcharge, and a third or later offense within five years of the last one adds four points.
A first reckless driving offense can mean up to sixty days in jail, and fines double in work zones and in sixty-five zones for speeding ten or more over the limit.

Injuring a vulnerable road user you failed to pass with care costs five hundred dollars and two points, an open container costs two hundred, and ignoring a request to light the compartment costs fifty.

hooks_spoken: Not clearing snow or ice costs twenty-five to seventy-five dollars, and ice that flies off and hurts someone or something can cost a private driver up to one thousand.
Leaving a car on a limited-access highway for four hours or more without permission risks up to two years without driving, and doing it again risks up to five.
Hit-and-run with injury or death, insurance fraud, lying on an application and a stand-in license test can all bring fines and jail, and a boating DUI costs every driving privilege.
